fullText:
Airlines can sell more tickets than seats—and leave passengers with confirmed reservations at the gate.

Overbooking bets on no-shows. Under U.S. rules, airlines must seek volunteers first: accepting means negotiating a deal, not claiming automatic compensation for being bumped against your will. Volunteer payments have no legal ceiling.

The receipts: 14 CFR §250.5 bases eligible payments on fare and the replacement’s planned arrival—not departure delay. Within 1 hour: $0. More than 1 but less than 2 hours domestically, or less than 4 internationally: 200% of fare, capped at $1,075. At least 2 hours domestically or 4 internationally—or no replacement: 400%, capped at $2,150. Airlines may pay more. §§250.8–250.9 require written rights and cash/check payment that day, at that airport; within 24 hours if replacement transportation leaves before payment can be prepared.

Check the boundary: these rules cover scheduled departures from U.S. airports on aircraft designed for 30 or more passengers. Cancellations, qualifying smaller-plane substitutions, operational/safety weight restrictions on aircraft with 60 or fewer seats, and missed ticketing/check-in requirements can exclude payment. A downgrade brings an appropriate fare refund, not bumping compensation. Before volunteering, confirm the replacement seat, meal/hotel coverage, and voucher expiry, blackout dates and restrictions. Keep your booking and arrival schedule. If involuntarily bumped, request the written rights statement; you need not accept a voucher instead of money owed.​
